opus-5.5.text:
I think the core challenge is that the technology is moving much faster than our ability to understand it, and regulation fundamentally needs some kind of understanding to work. With most technologies you regulate, you have a pretty good sense of what the failure modes are. With frontier AI, we're often discovering capabilities after the model is already trained, sometimes after it's already deployed. So you're trying to write rules for a system whose properties you can't fully specify in advance.

Closely related to that is the measurement problem. If you want to say "models above a certain level of dangerous capability need these safeguards," you need reliable evaluations for those capabilities, and our evals are still pretty immature. They can tell you when a model *can* do something, but it's much harder to confidently say a model *can't* do something, because maybe you just didn't elicit it properly. And as models get smarter, there's the additional worry that they could behave differently when they know they're being tested.

Then there's the alignment piece, which is the part I spend most of my time on. Right now we don't have techniques that we know will scale to systems smarter than us. Things like RLHF work because humans can evaluate the outputs. Once the model is doing tasks that humans can't really judge well, that breaks down. So a regulator can't simply say "make sure your model is aligned," because nobody, including the labs, knows how to verify that robustly for very capable systems. A lot of what good regulation could do is require transparency, require that labs actually do the safety research and show their work, and create incentives for investing in alignment rather than racing purely on capabilities.

And finally there's the coordination aspect. Competitive pressure between companies, and between countries, pushes everyone to move faster than they'd otherwise choose to. Any single actor slowing down unilaterally doesn't solve much. So you need something that changes the incentives for everyone at once, and that's both politically hard and technically hard, because it has to be flexible enough to keep up with a field where what's state of the art changes every few months.

So if I had to put it in one sentence: we need to regulate something we can't yet fully measure, using safety techniques we haven't yet fully developed, in an environment where everyone feels pressure to go faster.

r001.rationale: The response mentions coordination across companies and countries, but does not identify ensuring that regulation of dangerous AI-building practices applies globally as a key challenge.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think the core challenge is that we're trying to regulate something where the people who understand it best don't actually agree on how dangerous it is or when the dangerous capabilities will show up. That's pretty unusual. With most technologies you regulate, you have a decent picture of the failure modes. With frontier models, we're still discovering what they can do after they've been trained, sometimes months after deployment.

So you end up with this tension. If you regulate based on what models can do today, you're probably fine for today, but you're writing rules for a target that moves every six to twelve months. If you try to regulate for what models might do in two or three years, you're legislating against capabilities that nobody can demonstrate yet, and that invites a lot of reasonable pushback about whether you're just making things up.

The approach I find most promising is to not try to specify the dangerous behaviors in advance, and instead focus on the process. Require that labs actually measure what their systems can do before and after deployment, that those measurements are done rigorously and ideally checked by someone outside the lab, and that there are pre-committed thresholds where certain capabilities trigger certain safeguards. That way the regulation can keep up, because the measurement is what's doing the work, not a static list of prohibited things.

But even that has a hard problem underneath it, which is that evaluation is really immature as a science. We don't yet have great ways to be confident a model doesn't have some capability. Absence of evidence in an eval is weak evidence of absence. And if your whole regulatory framework rests on evals, then the quality of the evals becomes a safety-critical thing, and right now that quality varies enormously. So I'd say a lot of the real work isn't writing the policy, it's building the technical foundations that would make the policy mean something.

The other piece I'd add is incentives. Any individual lab faces competitive pressure to move fast, and the costs of being careful are borne by that lab while the benefits are spread across everyone. That's a classic coordination problem, and it's exactly the kind of thing regulation is supposed to solve. But it only works if the rules apply to everyone who's actually at the frontier, and the frontier isn't confined to one country. So you need some degree of international coordination, and that's slow and hard in ways that have nothing to do with the technology.

r001.rationale: The response says rules must apply to everyone at the frontier, which spans countries, and calls for international coordination—communicating the challenge of making frontier AI regulation global.

astra-6.text:
I think the key challenge is that you’re trying to regulate something that’s changing very quickly, and where we don’t yet have a good way to measure all the risks we care about. You want rules that will still make sense for the next generation of systems, even if those systems can do things that today’s models can’t.

So a lot depends on developing good evaluations: how do we tell whether a system has dangerous capabilities, and what evidence should a developer have to provide before deploying it? You also need regulators with the technical expertise and access to actually assess that evidence. Otherwise, you risk having rules that look reassuring on paper but don’t tell you much about whether a system is safe.

r001.rationale: The response discusses rapidly changing systems, measuring risks, evaluations, and regulator expertise, but does not identify global application of regulation on dangerous AI-building methods as a key challenge.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key challenge is that you’re trying to regulate something that’s changing very quickly, and where a lot of the risks are still poorly understood. You need enough technical understanding to distinguish requirements that actually make systems safer from requirements that just create paperwork.

So I’d focus on giving regulators the ability to see what’s happening at the frontier: what capabilities these systems have, how they’re being tested, and what evidence developers have that they can deploy them safely. And then you need a way to update the requirements as we learn more. If you wait until the risks are obvious to everyone, you may have waited too long.

r001.rationale: The response discusses adapting regulation to fast-changing technology and poorly understood risks, but does not identify global application of rules against dangerous ways of building AI as a key challenge.
